extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and examiners evaluating U.S. §101 eligibility (especially for software/GUI patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether asserted patent claims are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the Supreme Court's two-step Alice/Mayo framework, with attention to software and graphical user interface claims and the standards for resolving eligibility on Rule 12 motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step one — directed to ineligible concept
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, determine whether a patent claim is "directed to" a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea. (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217; Mayo, 566 U.S. at 70–73.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to one of these exceptions, proceed to step two. In software cases, the inquiry often asks whether the claims focus on specific asserted improvements in computer capabilities or instead on an abstract process for which computers are invoked merely as a tool (TecSec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-specific step-one rubric — specific computer improvement vs abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: In software cases, ask whether the claims "focus on specific asserted improvements in computer capabilities or instead on a process or system that qualifies [as] an abstract idea for which computers are invoked merely as a tool." (TecSec, Inc. v. Adobe Inc., 978 F.3d 1278, 1293.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely improving a user's experience while using a computer application is not, without more, sufficient to render claims patent-eligible (Customedia). Claims that recite generic presentation/selection/organization of information without a technical improvement will be treated as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that collect/organize/display information on generic computers are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to presenting, selecting, filtering, organizing, or otherwise manipulating information (collection/organization/display) on a generic computer are commonly treated as abstract ideas (Electric Power Grp.; In re Killian; Intell. Ventures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere use of a computer to present a humanly comprehensible amount of information or to speed up an organizational process does not render the claim patent-eligible. Examples: presenting a map, having a user select a portion, and synchronizing a list—without a technical improvement—was held abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-oriented / functional claim language is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: "A claim that merely describes an 'effect or result dissociated from any method by which [it] is accomplished' is usually 'not directed to patent-eligible subject matter.'" (Apple v. Ameranth, Inc., quoting Internet Pats. Corp. v. Active Network.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that use high-level functional verbs (presenting, receiving, selecting, synchronizing, applying, matching, determining, displaying, rearranging) without explaining how to accomplish those tasks are likely to be considered abstract. The specification should explain how to achieve the claimed result in a non-abstract way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation of manual processes using generic computers is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Automating a pre-existing manual procedure on a generic computer does not constitute a patentable improvement in computer technology (Credit Acceptance; Univ. of Fla. Rsch. Found.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed method could be performed by hand (e.g., with paper overlays, colored pencils, transparent sheets), then merely automating it on a computer is an Alice-type abstract idea. The claim must recite a technical solution beyond 'do it on a computer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step two — inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, at step two determine whether the claim includes an "inventive concept" sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice: whether the claims do 'significantly more' than simply describe the abstract method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis asks whether the additional features are more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Mere recitation of generic computer components or restatement of the abstract goal does not suffice (Intell. Ventures I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components and conventional activity do not supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that add only generic computer components or recite conventional, well-understood computer activities fail to provide an inventive concept (BASCOM; Apple; BSG Tech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat additions such as 'information handling system', 'computer program product', or generic synchronization as insufficient unless the claim provides a specific technical solution, tailored software, or particular programming that improves computer functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible and specific factual allegations required to survive Rule 12
rubrics_metrics.description: On a Rule 12 motion, courts accept the facts alleged in the complaint as true, but the patentee must present plausible, specific factual allegations that aspects of the claims are inventive in order to defeat a motion to dismiss (Aatrix; Cellspin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusory allegations of inventiveness, divorced from the claims or specification, are insufficient. Examples of adequate allegations: specific descriptions of unconventional hardware/software structures or novel data-transmittance that are discussed in the specification and complaint (Cellspin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations known in prior art cannot supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that is acknowledged as known in the prior art cannot be relied on as an inventive concept (e.g., 'user determined shape' was known in the prior art for map-selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification or prosecution history admits the limitation was known, that limitation cannot convert an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter at step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant post-solution activity does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements that are merely post-solution activity (e.g., a synchronization step stated without instruction) are insignificant if they add nothing more than conventional computer implementation (Apple, Two-Way Media context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will disregard such limitations if the claim provides no technical details on how to implement the post-solution activity beyond using generic components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must improve the functioning of the computer itself or disclose specific technical implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patent-eligible, claims should recite an improvement in computer functioning (make it operate more efficiently, solve a technological problem) or provide specific programming/tailored software/meaningful implementation guidance (Enfish/Core Wireless/Intell. Ventures contrast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely organizing information to help a user process it more quickly does not necessarily improve computer functionality. The specification should repeatedly emphasize the technical problem and how the claim elements solve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem specificity — is the problem specific to computing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the problem the claim addresses is specific to computing environments (e.g., limitations of small screens, interaction constraints) or whether the problem also existed in the non-computer (paper) world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem and the claimed solution are essentially the same as long-standing manual techniques (cartography, paper layering), that favors a finding of abstractness; if the specification shows solutions particular to computers or devices (as in Core Wireless), that supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate and procedural standards for Rule 12 §101 decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court's determination of patent eligibility under §101 is a question of law reviewed de novo on appeal, but the inquiry may contain underlying factual issues. On Rule 12(c)/(b)(6), courts take complaint allegations as true and must accept plausible factual allegations relevant to eligibility (Cellspin; Aatrix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review should ensure district courts do not ignore plausible, specific factual allegations of inventiveness. However, conclusory or unsupported inventiveness assertions are insufficient to defeat dismissal (Cellspin, Simio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Wireless exception — specific, repeated specification emphasis on computer improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to particular or specific implementations of presenting information on electronic devices that are repeatedly emphasized by the specification as improving device functioning (e.g., solving navigation on small screens) can be patent-eligible (Core Wireless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To benefit from Core Wireless, the specification must 'clearly indicate' that the claims are directed to an improvement in the functioning of computers or device-specific problems; mere broad claims about layering or display without device-specific technical detail will not suffice.
